prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a textbook case of progress being limited by how well we can measure. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removed the trap-induced light shift, which let thousands of atoms be interrogated at once, and Ye's group at JILA turned that into fractional systematic uncertainty and stability near 1e-18, with many-body effects (collisions, spin-orbit coupling, correlated or entangled ensembles) brought under control rather than merely avoided. The evidence is the kind I trust. Independent groups in Japan, France, Germany, the US, China and elsewhere reproduce the performance, and clock-to-clock frequency-ratio campaigns and fibre-linked comparisons agree at the level the claims require. The achievement has already opened new uses: millimetre- to centimetre-scale gravitational redshift sensing and relativistic geodesy, tighter limits on drifts of fundamental constants and on ultralight dark matter, and a credible route to redefining the SI second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, since all eight opening ballots proposed exactly Katori and Ye. The prior prizes (Hall and Hansch in 2005 for the comb, Wineland and Haroche in 2012 for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks) recognised enabling tools and a different platform, so this is a distinct step. Eight members ranked it, and five placed it in their top three, which is notable for a measurement-science result among condensed-matter and particle-physics ballots.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology might be seen as an accumulation of many incremental improvements shared across a large community (Lemonde, Gill, Schmidt, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto, Ovsiannikov and others), so a two-name prize inevitably leaves out people whose work was decisive for particular milestones, and the ion-clock lineage sits next to it. A second point is timing: the SI second has not yet been redefined, and some will argue the committee should wait for that societal consequence. Finally, the physics is a refinement of established atomic physics, not the opening of a new regime of matter, which is why condensed-matter colleagues rank moire or topological systems higher.

responses.point: Ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first: the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction plus the 2018 correlated-insulator and superconducting states opened moire matter, with a natural theory-plus-experiment trio, and he places optical lattice clocks only eighth.
responses.response: I accept the originality argument for B015; a new tunable platform for correlated electrons is a real opening of a field, and I would put it as my strongest alternative. But a few things hold me back from preferring it. Olle himself notes that the superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated, and the experimental credit is a sensitivity because Yuan Cao and co-leads are outside the credited names. The existence of the flat-band phases is reproducible, but the sample-to-sample variability in twist-angle disorder is well known, and I would want to know how much is firmly characterised. By contrast, the clock claim is a number that other laboratories can and do check against their own. I do not think a field-opening argument automatically outweighs a decisive, quantified improvement that has already changed what can be measured, and I hope the eighth place for clocks reflects that the metrology case has not been argued in detail yet.

responses.point: Ranks optical lattice clocks first as precision atomic physics where theory and experiment agree, notes that a two-person prize is clean, flags credit-boundary risk from Lemonde, Gill and the NIST groups, and observes that confirmation across laboratories makes recognition timely rather than premature.
responses.response: I agree with Eva on the core case and on timeliness, and I would add one qualification to her credit-boundary point. The risk is real but manageable: Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice demonstration, and Ye's pushing of stability and accuracy to the 1e-18 regime, are separable, documented contributions, whereas the others she names refined or reproduced specific milestones. Where I would press her is on what the citation should emphasise. I think it should name the magic-wavelength lattice concept and the resulting accuracy, not the future redefinition of the second, so that the prize does not depend on a metrological decision the committee cannot predict. I would also want the committee to avoid describing the clock as a spin-off of the frequency comb, since that would blur the distinction from the 2005 prize.

responses.point: Ranks magic-angle graphene first for its simple mechanism with universal consequences, and the maturity argument that recognition is timely, but places clocks only seventh, noting that the pending redefinition of the second could be a reason to wait.
responses.response: I take the point about waiting for the redefinition seriously, but I disagree that it is a reason to defer. The Nobel criterion is the discovery or invention, not the legal adoption of a standard, and the scientific case does not change if the CGPM acts in 2030 or later; the clocks have already been compared to better than the cesium definition in several independent laboratories. Waiting also has a cost, since the field is large and the credit picture gets harder, not easier, with time. On the simple-model argument for B015, I find it persuasive as science, but a continuum model that predicts a magic angle is a different strength of evidence from a measurement agreeing with a prediction at the 1e-18 level. I would not equate the elegance of a model with a larger discovery.

responses.point: Ranks magic-angle graphene first because it opened an entirely new experimental platform, ranks topological insulators second and optical lattice clocks third as a compact, defensible two-person configuration, noting the redefinition of the second is not yet complete.
responses.response: Eva's third place for clocks, with an explicit endorsement of the pair as defensible, is useful, since it means the disagreement among us is about the ordering of strong candidates, not about whether clocks are prize-worthy. I would push back gently on the idea that unfinished societal impact is a deficit: the physics is complete and the demonstration is global, and the societal application will follow. On B053, which she ranks second, I share the concern she herself raises: the credited names omit Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Molenkamp versus Hasan is a real choice, so a three-person limit forces an allocation I find harder to defend than the clock pair. That is part of why I would put topological insulators below clocks even though I recognise their conceptual weight.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first as the architecture for strong coupling, readout and essentially all superconducting processors, and acknowledges the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits creates a timing and balance question; he places clocks third.
responses.response: I agree with Goran that circuit QED is clean and mature, and I ranked it fourth for that reason; the demonstration of strong coupling and dispersive readout is a genuine physics result. My reservation is the 2025 prize, which recognised superconducting circuits so recently that a second circuits prize in 2026 would look unbalanced, and the Girvin and Devoret entanglement with the origin story makes the credit less tidy than Goran suggests. I would also argue that its impact is chiefly through quantum computing hardware, where the measure of success is still engineering scale-up. I note that I share an institutional neighbourhood with Goran through WACQT, and I have tried to avoid letting that push me either way.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to name only Katori and Ye, or whether the Lemonde, Gill or NIST groups are felt to be so decisive that a two-name prize would be considered incomplete.
How much weight to put on the unfinished redefinition of the second, and whether waiting would strengthen or weaken the case.
Whether magic-angle graphene (B015) will be judged more significant than a measurement-science result once the pairing mechanism and credit among experimental co-leads are better understood.
The precise framing of the citation so that it is distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict is apparent from my profile, but I disclose three connections. I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Jun Ye is a JILA scientist of the Hall group; I have no joint work with Ye or Katori that I can identify. My recent work on laser stabilisation with slow light touches ultrastable lasers, which are also central to clocks. I am on the WACQT executive team, which overlaps institutionally with Goran Johansson's Chalmers home, a connection that bears on B021 and not on my preferred B057.
